fields.meta_title: Newsletter Survey Builder for Reader Feedback | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a newsletter survey from a prompt: section ratings, signup questions, send-schedule votes, and staff newsletter checks. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Newsletter Survey That Shapes the Next Issue
fields.hero_description: Build a newsletter survey that asks readers what to keep, ties each answer to a subscriber, and saves it to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Into a Newsletter Survey
fields.features_subheading: Emergent builds the newsletter survey, the subscriber table behind it, and the alerts, then changes any of it when you prompt again.
fields.feature_1:
Questions drafted from your sections

Tell Emergent what the newsletter covers and what the answers should decide. It drafts a question for each section, and a follow-up prompt rewrites any question or adds one.
fields.feature_2:
Each answer saved to its subscriber

Every response saves as a row in a database you own, tagged with the subscriber's email address and the survey round. This January's section scores sit beside last January's.
fields.feature_3:
One question per screen on a phone

Anyone who taps through from an issue on a phone gets one question per screen, because Emergent can build the survey as a conversational flow with a large button for each rating.
fields.feature_4:
Answers synced to your email tool

The app connects to any email tool with an API. A signup answer can then land on that subscriber's record as a tag or a custom field, matched to the reader by email address.
fields.feature_5:
Low section scores sent to the editor

Pick the score that should reach an editor, and name that editor. The app emails them or posts in Slack with the section's ratings and every comment left about it in the survey.
fields.feature_6:
No cap on replies, and code you export

A survey sent to the whole list keeps every answer, with no response caps. On paid plans, the full code exports to your GitHub repository, ready to change or host anywhere.

fields.usecase_heading: How Four Newsletters Act on Survey Answers
fields.tab_content_1:
The lowest-rated section lands with the editor

Every January, The Tuesday Larder asks readers to rate its 5 sections from 1 to 5, and any section averaging under 3.0 goes to the editor. This year, Ask the Cook averaged 2.4 out of 5 from 412 answers, while every other section scored 3.8 or higher. Wren Halvorsen had its scores and comments that morning.
fields.tab_content_2:
Role and lane, tagged from the signup answers

Freight Brief asks every new subscriber 2 questions at signup: their role, and the freight lane they follow. In October, 196 of 240 new subscribers answered. Each answer saved to the subscriber's row as a tag, and the app synced the tags to the email tool. The ocean edition now goes only to readers who picked ocean.
fields.tab_content_3:
Twice a week won 318 of 530 reader votes

Parcel and Pine sends a daily gardening digest, and its footer asked readers how often they want it. Of 530 answers, 318 picked twice a week, 141 picked daily, and 71 picked weekly. The digest now goes out on Tuesday and Friday, and the footer question stays up to see whether the new schedule holds.
fields.tab_content_4:
Read rates by site show who misses the issue

Tallis Engineering sends a monthly staff newsletter to 900 people at the Dock Street plant and 2 offices. Its survey asked each person whether they read the last issue. At the plant, 18 of 64 said yes. At the offices, 132 of 177 did. Nadia Brennick in internal comms now prints a one-page edition for the plant break room.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Newsletter Survey
fields.howto_description: Follow these 7 steps to test and send a newsletter survey whose answers decide what the next issue covers.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Decide what the answers will change
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Ask about one thing per question
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Put the ratings before the comments
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down the decisions before you write a question: which section to cut, how often to send, which topics earn their own edition. A question that feeds none of them comes out. Put those decisions in your prompt, and Emergent drafts the survey around them.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Pew Research Center says double-barreled questions are difficult for respondents to answer. A question like "How are the recipes and photos?" becomes 2 ratings, one for each. Every score then points at one fix, and a low number tells the editor exactly what to change.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask the section ratings first and the open comment box last. Pew Research Center notes that the order in which questions are asked can influence how people respond. Keep the same order every year, and this year's scores compare fairly with last year's.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Answers tied to an email address can tag that reader in the email tool and get a reply. Anonymous answers cannot do either. Tell Emergent which you want, and it builds the survey to save the address with each answer or leave it out.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Send the draft to 5 readers before the full list. Pew Research Center calls pretesting an essential step in the questionnaire design process. Watch for a question they skip or answer in the comment box instead, and rewrite it before launch.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Put the link near the top of the issue
fields.howto_step_6_des: Place the survey link above the first story, not under the sign-off, and say how many questions it holds. Name the closing date in the issue. A week later, send one reminder to subscribers who have not answered yet.
fields.howto_step_7_des: In the first issue after the survey closes, share what readers said and what changes: the section that goes, the new send days. Run the same questions next year, and the scores show whether the change worked.

faq_plan.a: A newsletter survey is a short set of questions subscribers answer about the newsletter itself: what they read and what they want next. It can sit inside an issue or go out as its own email. The answers decide which sections stay and how often the newsletter goes out.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a newsletter survey?
faq_plan.a: Describe it in a prompt to Emergent's AI survey builder: the sections readers should rate, any signup or send-frequency questions, and who should hear about low scores. Emergent builds the survey, the database behind it, and the alerts. Put the link in your next issue, and answers start filling the table.

faq_plan.q: What newsletter survey questions should I ask?
faq_plan.a: Ask for one rating per section, how often readers want the newsletter, which topic they would add, and one open question about what to change. Add a role or industry question only if you will use it to split editions. Each question should feed a decision you can name before the survey goes out.

faq_plan.q: Is a newsletter survey template enough, or should I write my own?
faq_plan.a: A template is a fair start, but rename its questions after your own sections: a rating for each named section tells you more than one general satisfaction score. If the newsletter has a playful voice, an opener in the style of funny survey questions can match it. Emergent drafts the survey from a description of your sections, with nothing generic to strip out.

faq_plan.q: How often should I send a reader survey?
faq_plan.a: Run the full reader survey once a year, in the same month. This year's scores then line up against last year's. Between those, ask a single question in an issue footer when one decision is open, such as send days. Save the long survey for the annual round.

faq_plan.q: How many questions should a newsletter survey have?
faq_plan.a: Keep the annual survey to about 10 questions: one rating per section, a frequency question, a topic question, and one open comment box at the end. Tell readers the count in the issue. A footer question in a regular issue should stay a single question with 3 or 4 choices.

faq_plan.q: Should a newsletter survey use rating scales or yes or no answers?
faq_plan.a: Use a 1 to 5 rating scale when you want to rank sections against each other, since a yes or no only tells you whether a reader opens a section. For a fast check inside one issue, a short yes no questions survey with 3 or 4 items keeps answering to a few taps.

faq_plan.q: How do I get more subscribers to answer a newsletter survey?
faq_plan.a: Say in the issue how long the survey takes, and tell readers what last year's answers changed: the section you cut, the send day you moved. A reader who saw answers change the newsletter has a reason to answer again. Surveys built on Emergent have no response caps, and every subscriber who answers is counted.

faq_plan.q: Should a newsletter survey be anonymous?
faq_plan.a: Go anonymous only when you will never need to know who answered. Qualtrics describes anonymous responses as completely separate from any kind of personally identifiable information, while confidential responses are connected to personal information. Tie answers to subscribers when you want to tag or reply to readers, and keep sensitive topics anonymous.

faq_plan.q: Can I run a newsletter survey for an internal staff newsletter?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Ask whether people read the last issue and which section helped them, and save the site or team with each answer to see where the newsletter goes unread. Keep it about the newsletter: questions about how managers lead belong in a separate leadership survey. Each answer saves to a database you own.

plan.angle: No top 10 in the workbook (Wave 3), and every AlsoAsked candidate drifts to paid surveys, mail surveys or newsletter design, so the searcher is an editor or marketer who wants to ask subscribers something and act on it. Template pages list questions; none shows what an editor changes when the answers come back. This page shows four newsletter surveys built from a prompt, each ending in one editorial change: the lowest-rated section going to the editor, signup answers tagging each new subscriber for the email tool, a send-schedule question that moves a daily digest to two sends a week, and a staff newsletter survey that finds the one site that rarely reads it. The FAQ answers what a builder asks next: which questions, templates, how often, how many, scales versus yes or no, response rates, anonymity, and internal newsletters.
tab_stories: The Tuesday Larder, a weekly cooking newsletter, asks readers each January to rate its 5 sections from 1 to 5, and Pantry Q&A averages 2.4 from 412 answers while the other 4 sections score 3.8 or higher, so the editor, Wren Halvorsen, gets that section's scores and comments.

Freight Brief, a logistics newsletter, asks every new subscriber 2 questions at signup, their role and the lane they ship, and 196 of 240 October signups answer, so each subscriber row carries 2 tags that sync to the connected email tool.
Parcel and Pine, a daily gardening digest, puts one question in the footer asking how often readers want it, and 318 of 530 answers pick twice a week, so the digest moves to Tuesday and Friday sends.

Tallis Engineering surveys 900 staff about the monthly internal newsletter, and only 18 of 64 answers from the Dock Street plant say they read the last issue, against 70% or more at the 2 offices, so Nadia Brennick in internal comms adds a printed page for the plant break room.

scope.evidence: H1 'Build a Newsletter Survey That Shapes the Next Issue'; hero 'Build a newsletter survey that asks readers what to keep, ties each answer to a subscriber, and saves it to a database you own.'

intent.evidence: Covers questions to ask (FAQ 3, FAQ 6), template (FAQ 4), a 7-step how-to, and four worked surveys an editor acts on; no SERP in workbook, plan angle followed.

specificity.evidence: Editor vocabulary: 'section ratings', 'issue footer', 'send days', 'freight lane', 'print a one-page edition for the plant break room'.

openers.evidence: Feature bodies open on full sentences: 'Tell Emergent what the newsletter covers', 'Every response saves as a row', 'Pick the score that should reach an editor'.

craft.evidence: No blocking craft defect; repeated year-over-year and 'tell readers' ideas recorded as notes.

voice.evidence: Concrete details: 'Ask the Cook averaged 2.4 out of 5 from 412 answers', 'How are the recipes and photos?' split into 2 ratings, 'At the plant, 18 of 64 said yes'.

truth.evidence: Pew lines match their quoted spans (double-barreled 'difficult for respondents to answer', question order 'can influence how people respond', pretesting 'an essential step in the questionnaire design process'); Qualtrics anonymous/confidential lines match their spans; Emergent lines map to prompt-build, database-owned, conversational, api-connect, alerts, no-caps, code-export, free-start; 318+141+71=530; 96+81=177 and 74+58=132.

distinct.evidence: Newsletter-only stories (section scores, signup tags, send frequency, staff newsletter read rates); yes no questions survey, funny survey questions and leadership survey are linked, not targeted.
